newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian savings intentions fall in August.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian savings intentions fall in August.

text.p: Australian household savings intentions fell substantially in August from the highs of Febrary and May, according to a study by Norwich Union and the Melbourne Institute released on Monday.
The index fell to 95.4 in August, after having held steady at 100.6 in February and May. However, the August 1996 reading was above the 91.1 index level of a year earlier.

Norwich's economics director, Hugh Hodges, said the drop in intentions was pretty much across the board, and the response to all four questions in the index suggested falling confidence in the future of the economy.
The leading indicator measures repondents views of their present financial situation, expected real income increases and the likelihood that they may cut spending and increase savings.
An index of 100 represents an equal balance of favourable and unfavourable opinions to the four questions.
The higher the index the more favourable the responses.

"Concerns about the effects of the federal budget would seem to be a key factor in the result, but it is important to note that the survey was conducted before the budsget when there was considerable speculation about some possible 'draconian' measures," Hodges said.
But he added that while the index had fallen, it was still relatively high.

Hodges said Norwich believed a good budget which would allay many concerns had been delivered, and were therefore cautious about drawing too many conclusions from the August fall as "the next survey may well reverse this fall."

The questions on household's present financial situation and assessment of their likelihood to save over the coming year were the positive contributors to the index. While down on February and May, most were still confident they can save, Norwich found.

The questions on the likelihood of households cutting spending and whether or not their income is expected to increase more than prices will have elicited pessimistic responses, as they have since the survey began in November 1993.
"Clearly the great majority of consumers have very little hope of their income going up much at all, particularly when it is recognised that inflation continues to be quite low," Hodges said.
The reasons for savings were little changed in August, with saving for the future or retirement the most important of the five alternatives put to households, Norwich said.
Over the past year savings for holidays or travel was the big mover, gaining through 1995 and peaking in May 1996 at 32 percent.

Norwich found more households saw superannuation as an asset, with about 50 percent nominating it as one. At 24 percent, shares/trusts held near their May high of 26 percent, while property remained near its average level of 14 percent.

"In addition, and while still the most mentioned of the assets at 56 percent, bank deposits may be slipping as this is the lowest proportion of households with bank deposits in any of our surveys," the report said.

When asked what was the best thing to do with new savings, shares reached a new high of 14 percent. The average preference rate for the last four surveys gave shares an average rating of nearly 13 percent, compared to eight percent a year earlier.
Other choices were more stable, but real estate has lost preference for some time, Norwich said.

The latest four quarter average is 21 percent, compared to 25 percent a year earlier. The August reading of 21 percent was also well down from May 1994, when 33 percent of households thought real estate was the best thing to do with new savings.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
